paragraphs.text: Ask most people to picture a lighthouse keeper and they will probably imagine a solitary figure with a beard and a pipe, gazing out at a stormy sea. It is an attractive picture, but it tells only a small part of the story. For generations, until machines took over their duties, keepers did demanding and often repetitive work on which the lives of sailors depended. Their days were shaped less by dramatic rescues than by routine, and the qualities their employers valued most were reliability and patience rather than courage.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The night was the heart of the job. Before electricity reached the coast, the light came from oil lamps whose wicks had to be trimmed regularly so that they burned brightly without smoking; American keepers were nicknamed 'wickies' for this reason. In many towers the great lens turned on a clockwork mechanism driven by a heavy weight, which slowly sank down the centre of the tower and had to be wound back up every few hours. If the keeper on watch fell asleep, the light could stop rotating, and a ship relying on its particular pattern of flashes might mistake one headland for another. For this reason, falling asleep on duty was treated as one of the most serious offences a keeper could commit.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Daylight brought a different set of tasks. Oil lamps left a thin film of soot on the lens and windows, and every surface had to be cleaned each morning, while brass fittings were polished and walls repainted to protect them from salt air. Keepers also kept detailed logbooks, recording the state of the light, passing vessels and, above all, the weather. The historian Eilidh Macrae, who examined logbooks from eleven Scottish stations, found that the entries suggested keepers spent more of their waking hours on cleaning and maintenance than on watching the light itself. She is careful to point out, however, that her sample came from a single region and may not reflect conditions elsewhere.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Where a keeper lived made an enormous difference to his life. At shore stations, built on headlands, keepers often lived with their wives and children in cottages beside the tower, and wives frequently shared the work, sometimes officially taking over when a husband died. Rock stations, built on isolated reefs or tiny islands, were another matter. Here only men were posted, usually in teams of three, so that if one fell ill or was injured the other two could continue to run the light. They typically worked several weeks at a time before a boat brought their replacements, although a long spell of bad weather could keep the relief boat away for days or even weeks beyond the planned date.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Living in such close quarters demanded tact. Gwilym Pritchard, who spent fourteen years on rock stations off the Welsh coast before retiring, recalls that small habits could become intensely irritating. 'You learned not to whistle the same tune twice,' he says. Cooking was shared on a rota, and a man who could not make a decent meal was not popular for long. To fill the quiet hours, keepers took up an impressive range of pastimes. Pritchard taught himself to repair clocks, while one of his colleagues built detailed model ships inside glass bottles. Some keepers grew vegetables in sheltered corners of the rock, although salt spray destroyed much of what they planted. Reading was almost universal, and books were exchanged so often that, as Pritchard puts it, 'every station had the same library by the end of the year.'
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Change came gradually and then very quickly. Electric lamps removed the need to tend flames, and from the middle of the twentieth century automatic equipment could switch lights on at dusk, change failed bulbs and report faults to a distant control room. One by one, stations lost their keepers, and in Britain the last of them left at the end of the 1990s. Some keepers stayed on as part-time attendants, visiting a light occasionally to check the equipment. Pritchard admits that he felt a mixture of relief and sadness when his last station was automated. 'The machines were more dependable than we were,' he says, 'but a machine never noticed a small boat in trouble.'
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The keepers' legacy is more than romantic. Many former stations now welcome visitors, and some cottages have been turned into holiday homes. Less obviously, the logbooks themselves have become valuable. Because keepers recorded wind, rain and sea conditions several times a day, often for decades at the same spot, their notes offer scientists a long and consistent record of the coastal climate. Researchers studying how coastal storms have changed over time increasingly turn to these handwritten pages, some of which describe places where no official weather station was ever built. In that sense, the keepers are still keeping watch.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Life Behind the Lamp

A. Ask most people to picture a lighthouse keeper and they will probably imagine a solitary figure with a beard and a pipe, gazing out at a stormy sea. It is an attractive picture, but it tells only a small part of the story. For generations, until machines took over their duties, keepers did demanding and often repetitive work on which the lives of sailors depended. Their days were shaped less by dramatic rescues than by routine, and the qualities their employers valued most were reliability and patience rather than courage.

B. The night was the heart of the job. Before electricity reached the coast, the light came from oil lamps whose wicks had to be trimmed regularly so that they burned brightly without smoking; American keepers were nicknamed 'wickies' for this reason. In many towers the great lens turned on a clockwork mechanism driven by a heavy weight, which slowly sank down the centre of the tower and had to be wound back up every few hours. If the keeper on watch fell asleep, the light could stop rotating, and a ship relying on its particular pattern of flashes might mistake one headland for another. For this reason, falling asleep on duty was treated as one of the most serious offences a keeper could commit.

C. Daylight brought a different set of tasks. Oil lamps left a thin film of soot on the lens and windows, and every surface had to be cleaned each morning, while brass fittings were polished and walls repainted to protect them from salt air. Keepers also kept detailed logbooks, recording the state of the light, passing vessels and, above all, the weather. The historian Eilidh Macrae, who examined logbooks from eleven Scottish stations, found that the entries suggested keepers spent more of their waking hours on cleaning and maintenance than on watching the light itself. She is careful to point out, however, that her sample came from a single region and may not reflect conditions elsewhere.

D. Where a keeper lived made an enormous difference to his life. At shore stations, built on headlands, keepers often lived with their wives and children in cottages beside the tower, and wives frequently shared the work, sometimes officially taking over when a husband died. Rock stations, built on isolated reefs or tiny islands, were another matter. Here only men were posted, usually in teams of three, so that if one fell ill or was injured the other two could continue to run the light. They typically worked several weeks at a time before a boat brought their replacements, although a long spell of bad weather could keep the relief boat away for days or even weeks beyond the planned date.

E. Living in such close quarters demanded tact. Gwilym Pritchard, who spent fourteen years on rock stations off the Welsh coast before retiring, recalls that small habits could become intensely irritating. 'You learned not to whistle the same tune twice,' he says. Cooking was shared on a rota, and a man who could not make a decent meal was not popular for long. To fill the quiet hours, keepers took up an impressive range of pastimes. Pritchard taught himself to repair clocks, while one of his colleagues built detailed model ships inside glass bottles. Some keepers grew vegetables in sheltered corners of the rock, although salt spray destroyed much of what they planted. Reading was almost universal, and books were exchanged so often that, as Pritchard puts it, 'every station had the same library by the end of the year.'

F. Change came gradually and then very quickly. Electric lamps removed the need to tend flames, and from the middle of the twentieth century automatic equipment could switch lights on at dusk, change failed bulbs and report faults to a distant control room. One by one, stations lost their keepers, and in Britain the last of them left at the end of the 1990s. Some keepers stayed on as part-time attendants, visiting a light occasionally to check the equipment. Pritchard admits that he felt a mixture of relief and sadness when his last station was automated. 'The machines were more dependable than we were,' he says, 'but a machine never noticed a small boat in trouble.'

G. The keepers' legacy is more than romantic. Many former stations now welcome visitors, and some cottages have been turned into holiday homes. Less obviously, the logbooks themselves have become valuable. Because keepers recorded wind, rain and sea conditions several times a day, often for decades at the same spot, their notes offer scientists a long and consistent record of the coastal climate. Researchers studying how coastal storms have changed over time increasingly turn to these handwritten pages, some of which describe places where no official weather station was ever built. In that sense, the keepers are still keeping watch.
